abstract: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a life-threatening vascular disease lacking effective pharmacotherapy. The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) innate immune pathway has been linked to inflammatory conditions, yet its role in AAA remains unclear. Here, we combined single-cell transcriptomics, mouse models, pharmacological inhibition, and human tissue validation to investigate the role of this pathway in AAA. In murine single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data, cGAS-STING activation was predominantly observed in AAA endothelial cells (ECs). Human scRNA-seq and scissor-based classification of stable versus ruptured AAAs showed that cGAS and STING1 were significantly upregulated in ECs from ruptured AAA, implicating pathway activation in rupture risk. Bioinformatic analyses suggested that endothelial cGAS-STING activation correlates with barrier dysfunction and oxidative stress, and that dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) deficiency may link DNA damage to pathway activation. In Angiotensin II (Ang II) -induced murine AAA, cGAS, p-STING, and p-TBK1 were markedly elevated. Pharmacological blockade with RU.521 (cGAS inhibitor) or STING-IN-2 (STING antagonist) reduced AAA incidence, aortic dilation, and structural damage, while improving endothelial mitochondrial morphology. In human AAA tissues, immunohistochemistry (IHC) confirmed increased cGAS, STING, and TBK1 expression. Moreover, RU.521 or STING-IN-2 treatment of patient-derived 3D AAA organoids significantly downregulated cGAS, p-STING, and p-TBK1, confirming target engagement. Collectively, our findings indicate that the cGAS-STING pathway is activated in murine and human AAA, and that targeting this axis may offer a promising therapeutic approach to limit AAA progression.
